title: Can a robot nail wall sheathing to code tolerance, and what decides it?
lede: research programme on robotic sheathing of a wood-frame wall; milestone 1: APA's 1/8 in gap shrinks the joint-nail window to ±3.14 mm and sheets must hang plumb to about 0.03°; milestone 2: a bowed stud moves under the straight sheet edge, so at published stud warp a robot reading each stud once gets 55% clean sheets, three reads 80% and perfect sensing 87%, while a 3x or doubled 2x at the joints (as the shear-wall standard allows) gives 100% with three reads; milestone 4: tacking the sheet and aiming from its measured edge lets a robot hang it to 0.54° and 10 mm (1σ) on doubled joints, 18 times coarser than the 0.03° single-2x joints need, where re-hanging tops out at 87% clean; milestone 3 (first part, MuJoCo): a sheet lowered onto a ledger and released seats to 0.0001° if the robot presses under about 100 N, and then PS 2 panel squareness leaves 100% clean sheets on doubled joints but at most 84–95% on single 2x; milestone 3 (second part): a stock Unitree G1 holds at most 8.7 kg and an H1 18.8 kg, so neither can carry the 21.8 kg sheet, but on the ledger both press it (66–110 N, 128–281 N) and at Unitree's own joint gains both are soft enough for the ledger to seat it, except an H1 with a rigid clamp; push below W/(2μ) when sliding it or it tips; milestone 5: with every stage of the cycle charged (place, sense, nail, re-drive missed nails), two 2x at the joint and one read a stud give 99.97% clean sheets in 76–216 s, while the best single-2x pipeline gets 56% and is 18–65 s slower a sheet, which is what the extra joint stud may cost to frame
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) asking whether a stock humanoid, a mobile manipulator with a lift or a purpose-built gantry can hang a 4x8 sheet of wall sheathing and land all 62 nails where the panel maker and the code want them, which error source decides it, and what a clean sheet costs; it gathers track 20's 26 buildbot-* projects into one question aimed at Automation in Construction. Milestone 1 adds what earlier projects left out: panels are hung with a 1/8 in gap (APA's recommendation) centred on the joint stud, sheets are hung slightly off and out of plumb, and their width differs from the 48 in stud module. With the gap, the 34 joint nails' window shrinks from ±3.93 to ±3.14 mm, and the single stud reading needed for 95% clean sheets (0.9 mm tool scatter) falls from 0.90 to 0.41 mm; at buildbot-studfind's 0.89 mm only 75% of sheets come out clean, 56% if the robot does not plan for the gap. With a 0.5 mm stud reading, a robot aiming at the design window has no tolerance for sheet pose at all; aiming from the measured sheet edge (to 0.5 mm) allows 0.44 mm of translation and 0.031° of rotation (1σ), and halves the weight of the stud error. Along a 40 ft wall, sheets butted with a 1/8 in gauge drift 3.2 mm a sheet: no third sheet is clean with full panels, and panels trimmed 1/16 in keep a joint window for four sheets; setting each sheet from its own studs keeps every sheet at 98% clean. Milestone 2 lets the studs bow and twist as real lumber does. A Stud-grade 8 ft 2x4 may bow 3/4 in and twist 3/8 in, and published kiln-dried studs average 0.11–0.21 in of bow and 0.08–0.16 in of twist. Bow moves the 1.5 in nailing face under a sheet edge that stays straight, so a single-2x joint closes for any bow over 0.53 in, whatever the robot knows. At the lower published warp, one read per stud gives 55% clean sheets, three reads and a fitted curve 80%, perfect stud and edge sensing 87%; reaching 95% would mean rejecting about two thirds of studs for bow. Framing the joints with a 3x or two fastened 2x (named for adjoining panel edges in the shear-wall standard, SDPWS 4.3.7.1) widens the window by 1/2 in a side, and three reads then give 100% clean sheets at both warp levels; twist costs 1–2 points. Milestone 4 asks how coarsely a robot may hang the sheet if it tacks it with two field nails, measures where the edge landed and aims the joint nails from that, or re-hangs it when the window looks too tight. On single-2x joints the sheet must still hang to about 0.03° and 0.4 mm (1σ) for 95% clean sheets; re-hanging a 1 mm / 0.1° hang peaks at 87% (2.1 hangs a sheet), and a held sheet may sway only 0.19 mm under the nail. On two 2x fastened at the joint, tack-then-measure allows 0.54° and 10 mm at the lower published warp, and a held sheet may sway 4.1 mm: the placement target for the humanoid and lift experiments. Milestone 3, first part asks whether a ledger board under the sheet can do the squaring a robot cannot. In MuJoCo, a 21.8 kg sheet lowered 0.25–2° off plumb onto a level ledger and released ends within 0.0001° of it for any press up to 100 N; above 115–380 N (wall friction 0.7 to 0.2) friction holds the whole error, at 0.87–0.99 of the closed form, and a wrist that keeps over about 7,500 N·m/rad of stiffness at 1° keeps part of its own error. Seated, what is left is the panel (PS 2-18: 0.083° out of square, a 1/16 in edge bow that rocks it up to 0.149°) and a laser line rated 1/8 in at 30 ft: 100% clean sheets on doubled joints in every setting, 84–86% on single 2x with panels drawn up to the PS 2 limits, and 95% only if panels are within a quarter of them. Milestone 3, second part puts a stock Unitree G1 or H1 (MuJoCo Menagerie, static whole-body model, torque limits, no foot slip) in that holder's place. Neither can carry the sheet to the wall: the G1 holds at most 2.8–8.7 kg in both hands at 0.6–1.3 m and the H1 12.4–18.8 kg. With the sheet on the ledger, the G1 presses 66–110 N and the H1 128–281 N. Sliding the seated sheet to its stud line tips it unless pushed below W/(2μl) (MuJoCo within 1.6% in 14 cases); a G1 manages the slide at ledger friction 0.3 but not 0.5, and not through palm friction at all. At Unitree's published joint gains (G1 arms 60 N·m/rad) the sheet's stiffness about the landing corner is 2.9 to 31 times under the limit at which a hold keeps its error, so the ledger seats it; only an H1 with a rigid clamp is too stiff (it keeps 0.46–0.99° of a 1° error). The catch: that softness would let the sheet's weight turn a hold 10–14° if the ledger did not carry it. Hang and sway errors are swept, not measured on a robot; the humanoid model is static with gains taken as its only compliance, and the panel distributions within PS 2's limits are assumed. Monte Carlo checked against buildbot-studfind and closed forms. Stud, edge, gauge and width errors are swept, not measured; the gap, edge distance and trim come from APA pages seen in search results; stud warp means and limits come from search snippets of USDA and Wood and Fiber reports, the warp distribution shape is assumed (two are shown), and nothing is tested on hardware. Milestone 5 puts the stages in one steady-state cycle along a row: a lift stands the sheet on the ledger, the robot slides, presses and tacks it, reads the three new studs and both edges, nails with edge aim (timed by buildbot-mobilebase, 54 or 121 s) and re-drives every missed nail. On two 2x at the joint a single read a stud gives 0.9997 first-pass clean sheets at the lower warp and is the fastest choice in all 108 swept time cells: 76–216 s a sheet. On single 2x no sensing policy passes 0.59 (0.7–2.2 nails missed a sheet), three reads are fastest, and the best sheet is 17.8–65.2 s slower, all of it rework: at 30 s a re-driven nail, framing the extra joint stud may take 30–42 s a sheet and still win. Firing without waiting out a 4 N·s recoil costs up to 7.6 points of clean sheets on single 2x (a conservative model) and nothing on doubled joints, and on doubled joints a lift that hangs and tacks the sheet to 0.25° and 5 mm needs no ledger (0.978). Every stage time except the nailing is swept, not measured.
